question: When the seven members of the Swiss Federal Council deal with an item of business at their meeting, how do they proceed to a decision?

options.A: The President tables a proposal and the other six members confirm it unless three of them object.
options.B: The members vote first on the available options, and the majority position becomes the Federal Council's decision.
options.C: The item is first referred to the cantons for a consultative vote, and the Federal Council then implements the result.
options.D: The members first seek a common solution, and only vote if they fail to reach one.

source_quote: They discuss the items on the agenda at the Federal Council meeting and seek a common solution. Only if it does not reach a solution, does the Federal Council vote.
notes: Consensus-before-vote is the defining feature of the Swiss collegial executive; no majority-vote casting exists in the normal case.

question: To force an optional referendum against a law passed by the Swiss Parliament, how many valid signatures must be collected, and within what deadline?

options.A: 100,000 signatures within 100 days
options.B: 50,000 signatures within 18 months
options.C: 100,000 signatures within 18 months
options.D: 50,000 signatures within 100 days

source_quote: collect 50,000 valid signatures within 100 days of the publication of the new legislation
notes: Pair with K011: the optional referendum is 50,000 signatures / 100 days; the federal popular initiative is 100,000 / 18 months.

question: A campaign team is gathering signatures for an optional referendum against a federal law. Which restriction applies to the individual signature lists?

options.A: Each list must carry at least 500 signatures from one and the same canton.
options.B: A single list may only contain signatures from people of the same commune, because the communes are the first to check the signatures.
options.C: A voter may sign only one list per canton, and any duplicate signature invalidates the whole list.
options.D: Each list must be countersigned by the mayor of the commune before it can be submitted.

source_quote: A further requirement is that any given signature list may contain only the signatures of persons from the same commune – because the communes are the first to check the signatures.
notes: Counter-intuitive administrative detail: signature gathering is decentralised to the commune for verification. The same per-commune form rule applies to popular initiatives.

question: How many valid signatures must be collected for a federal popular initiative, and within what time limit?

options.A: 50,000 signatures within 100 days
options.B: 100,000 signatures within 18 months
options.C: 100,000 signatures within 100 days
options.D: 50,000 signatures within 18 months

source_quote: For an initiative to come to fruition, it must be signed by 100,000 voters within 18 months.
notes: Direct democracy threshold. Contrast with K007: referendum 50,000 / 100 days.

question: Across the Swiss cantons, who presides over the cantonal government, and what does that role carry with it?

options.A: The population of the canton elects a cantonal president directly for a four-year term, with decision-making powers equal to those of the other members.
options.B: The Federal Council appoints a cantonal president for a two-year term.
options.C: The presidency passes to the longest-serving member and carries substantial additional powers.
options.D: The presidency usually rotates from year to year and carries no privileges beyond chairing the cantonal government's meetings.

source_quote: Cantonal governments usually have a different president each year - the position rotating according to the length of time the government members have been in office. The president does not enjoy any special privileges or status, apart from chairing cantonal government meetings.
notes: CANTONAL-VARIABLE: rotation follows length of service, so the source says 'usually'. Phrased as the general cantonal pattern, never as a universal seven-member rule.

question: When the cantonal majority is counted for a constitutional amendment or a vote on joining a supranational community, what weight does each of the former half-cantons carry?

options.A: A full vote, the same as any other canton.
options.B: No vote at all, since they are no longer separate cantons.
options.C: Half a vote each.
options.D: Two votes each, reflecting their combined historic weight.

source_quote: The votes of the former half-cantons of Obwalden, Nidwalden, Basel-Stadt, Basel-Landschaft, Appenzell Ausserrhoden and Appenzell Innerrhoden each count as half a vote.
notes: The six former half-cantons weigh 0.5 each, so the cantonal majority is effectively a weighted 23-canton vote. Note this is a separate mechanism from the single Council of States seat they hold.

question: In Switzerland, what is the shortest notice period that can validly be agreed for terminating a tenancy?

options.A: One month for residential premises and three months for commercial premises
options.B: Two months for residential premises and four months for commercial premises
options.C: Three months for residential premises and six months for commercial premises
options.D: Three months for residential premises only, with no statutory minimum for commercial premises

source_quote: In einem Mietvertrag muss die Kündigungsfrist mindestens drei Monate für Wohnräume und sechs Monate für Geschäftsräume betragen, es können aber auch längere Fristen vereinbart werden.
notes: Source quote is German (official Canton Bern conciliation-authority page); English rendering in the question: in a rental agreement the notice period must be at least three months for residential premises and six months for commercial premises, and longer periods may be agreed. Commonly cited German practice of one month's notice plus end-of-month termination is NOT the Swiss rule.

question: Under Swiss federal law, what residence requirement must be met before applying for ordinary naturalisation?

options.A: At least five years of residence, including one of the two years preceding the application
options.B: At least ten years of residence, all of it within the five years preceding the application
options.C: At least fifteen years of residence, including five of the ten years preceding the application
options.D: At least ten years of residence, including three of the five years prior to the application being made

source_quote: Federal law requires you to have lived in Switzerland for at least ten years, including three of the five years prior to the application being made.
notes: CANTONAL-VARIABLE: on top of the federal ten-year rule, each canton sets an additional requirement of between two and five years' residence in the particular commune or canton, and each commune makes its own rules within cantonal and federal law. Those extra conditions are deliberately not tested here.

question: Which Swiss residence permit must a foreign citizen already hold before being able to apply for ordinary naturalisation?

options.A: A short-term residence permit (L)
options.B: A residence permit (B)
options.C: A settlement permit (C)
options.D: A cross-border commuter permit (G)

source_quote: Holders of a settlement permit (C permit)
notes: Ordinary naturalisation is restricted to holders of a C permit; the residency periods themselves are tested separately. Simplified naturalisation is open to other categories (spouse or child of a Swiss citizen, stateless minor, third-generation residents under 25).

question: A learner obtains a Swiss provisional driving licence on their 19th birthday. How long must they wait before they may take the practical driving test?

options.A: Six months
options.B: At least twelve months
options.C: At least twenty-four months
options.D: No fixed waiting period, once the compulsory traffic skills course has been attended

source_quote: If you get your provisional licence before your 20th birthday, you will need to wait at least 12 months before you can take the practical driving test.
notes: The 12-month wait is conditional on the provisional licence having been issued before the 20th birthday; the compulsory eight-hour traffic skills course is a separate precondition for registering for the test.

question: Two neighbouring communes in the same Swiss canton can levy different tax rates on an identical household income. What accounts for the difference?

options.A: Each commune determines its own tax co-efficient, and these co-efficients can vary considerably
options.B: Each canton sets a separate statutory tax rate for each individual commune within it
options.C: The Confederation adds a municipal surtax that differs from commune to commune
options.D: The statutory tax rate is fixed by federal law but is waived by individual communes

source_quote: Because each commune determines its own tax co-efficient, and these can vary considerably, there can be low-tax and high-tax communes within the same canton.
notes: COMMUNAL-VARIABLE: the co-efficient is changed from time to time, so no specific value is permanent. This is why there can be low-tax and high-tax communes within a single canton — a distinctly Swiss feature of communal tax autonomy.

question: For a residential rental in Switzerland, what is the maximum rental deposit (security deposit) a landlord may require?

options.A: One month's rent
options.B: Two months' rent
options.C: Three months' rent
options.D: There is no statutory maximum

source_quote: Rental deposit, also known as a security deposit: This must only be paid when required in the agreement. For residential rentals, this is a maximum of three months' rent.
notes: The deposit may be demanded only if the agreement provides for it; three months' rent is a ceiling, not an entitlement.

question: In Switzerland, a policyholder who wants to switch compulsory basic health insurer for the following calendar year must have the cancellation letter received by their current insurer by which date?

options.A: 15 October
options.B: 30 November
options.C: 15 December
options.D: 31 December

source_quote: Your letter must reach your current health insurer by 30 November.
notes: The 'Stichtag 30. November' is uniquely Swiss. Note the separate mid-year cancellation right that only holders of the CHF 300 standard deductible enjoy (tested separately in this category).

question: In Switzerland, a healthy adult who chooses the highest available compulsory basic health insurance deductible should set aside how much per year in order to be able to cover their own maximum share of healthcare costs?
source_quote:
You should still put CHF 3,200 aside in case you do fall ill
(CHF 2,500 deductible and CHF 700 retention fee).
notes: CHF 3,200 = highest adult deductible CHF 2,500 + CHF 700 maximum annual retention fee. A German/EU reader is likely to think only of a deductible.

question: Under Swiss compulsory basic health insurance, an adult holds the standard annual deductible of CHF 300. What is the maximum that this adult can end up paying out of pocket for healthcare in one calendar year?

options.A: CHF 700

source_quote: In other words, for an insured person with an annual deductible of CHF 300, the maximum cost share is CHF 1000 per calendar year.
notes: Key anti-trap item: CHF 1,000 is the MAXIMUM ANNUAL COST SHARE (CHF 300 deductible + CHF 700 maximum retention fee), not a deductible band. Distractor A is the retention-fee cap alone.

question: In Swiss compulsory basic health insurance, which set of optional annual deductible levels may adults choose from?
source_quote: For adults, the available deductibles are 500, 1000, 1500, 2000 and 2500 francs, and for children 100, 200, 300, 400, 500 and 600 francs.
notes: Levels are chosen voluntarily; there is no age / income ('affluence') / rural-residence rule assigning a band. Distractor B is the children's list.

question: In Swiss compulsory basic health insurance, a policyholder wants to move from the standard CHF 300 deductible to a higher optional deductible. When can that change take effect?

options.A: At any time during the year, on 30 days' notice
options.B: Only at the beginning of a calendar year
options.C: From 1 April, when insurers recalculate their premiums
options.D: Immediately, provided the policyholder has had no treatment in the current year

source_quote: A change in the level of the deductible can only take effect at the beginning of a calendar year.
notes: The deductible level is locked to the calendar year, unlike, for example, switching insurers. Do not confuse with the separate end-of-June cancellation right for CHF 300 deductible holders (S019).

question: In Switzerland, what is the maternity allowance during the 14 weeks of maternity leave following a birth?

options.A: 80 per cent of the mother's earnings, with no upper daily limit
options.B: 90 per cent of the mother's earnings, but no more than CHF 300 per day
options.C: 80 per cent of the mother's earnings, but no more than CHF 220 per day
options.D: 100 per cent of the mother's earnings, but no more than CHF 220 per week

source_quote:
Maternity allowance amounts to 80% of your
earnings, but no more than CHF 220 per day.
notes: Highly Swiss-specific 14-week / 80% / CHF 220-per-day package. Cantonal provisions, personnel regulations and collective employment contracts may provide more generous arrangements. Do not substitute EU maternity-benefit rates.

question: Is English an official language of Switzerland?

options.A: Yes — English became an official language of the Confederation in the 1938 constitutional revision that also recognised Romansh
options.B: Yes — English is an official language of the Confederation alongside German, French and Italian
options.C: No — it is not an official language, although it is widely used to bridge the country's linguistic divides
options.D: No — it is not an official language and is used in Switzerland only in the tourism sector

source_quote: Although it is not an official language, English is often used to bridge the divides, and a significant proportion of official documentation is available in English.
notes: Switzerland is not in the EU, and English has no federal status of any kind; the source is SWI swissinfo.ch quoted in the S047 file.

question: What is the lowest point in Switzerland, and in which canton is it located?

options.A: Lake Constance, in the canton of Thurgau, at 395 m
options.B: Lake Maggiore (Ticino), at 193 m
options.C: The Rhine gorge in the canton of Schaffhausen, at 302 m
options.D: Lake Neuchâtel, in the canton of Neuchâtel, at 372 m

source_quote: Lowest point: Lake Maggiore (Ticino) 193 m (633 feet)
notes: German-language readers often assume Lake Constance (Bodensee) is Switzerland's lowest point. The lowest point lies in Italian-speaking Ticino.

question: Apart from the canton of Ticino, in which part of Switzerland is Italian spoken?

options.A: In four southern valleys of the canton of Graubünden
options.B: In four southern valleys of the canton of Valais
options.C: In two southern valleys of the canton of Ticino and around the city of Lugano
options.D: In the Italian-speaking minority areas of the cantons of Fribourg and Geneva

source_quote: Italian is spoken in Ticino and four southern valleys of Canton Graubünden.
notes: Same source file flags this fact REGIONAL VARIABLE (language shares are population-statistics dependent); the named location itself is stable. Distinct from the Graubünden trilingual-canton fact.

question: According to the Swiss federal information portal, approximately what share of the population primarily speaks (Swiss-)German as its main language?

options.A: 0.5 per cent
options.B: 8 per cent
options.C: 23 per cent
options.D: 62 per cent

source_quote: 62 per cent of the population primarily speak (Swiss-)German, 23 per cent French, 8 per cent Italian and 0.5 per cent Romansh.
notes: Distractors are the neighbouring shares in the same sentence (French / Italian / Romansh) — the classic mix-up. Figures are rounded; Switzerland Tourism (S028) gives 62.6 % German, 22.9 % French, 8.2 % Italian, 0.5 % Romansh. Shares are population-statistics dependent and REGIONAL VARIABLE.

question: Roughly what proportion of Swiss communes have their own parliament?

options.A: Around a fifth
options.B: Around a third
options.C: Around a half
options.D: Around a tenth

source_quote: Around a fifth of Switzerland's communes have their own parliaments, and local laws relating to matters such as streets, school buildings, water and energy prices, as well as parking regulations.
notes: Where a commune has no parliament, the commune assembly decides in its place — the source page does not state this, so it is not asserted here.

question: What is the highest point in Switzerland, and in which mountain range is it located?

options.A: Dufour Peak, 4,634 m, in the Bernese Alps
options.B: Monte Rosa, 4,634 m, in the Pennine Alps
options.C: The Jungfrau, 4,158 m, in the Monte Rosa Mountains
options.D: Dufour Peak, 4,634 m, in the Monte Rosa Mountains

source_quote: Highest point: Dufour Peak, in the Monte Rosa Mountains, 4,634 m (15,203 feet)
notes: German- and Austrian-language readers commonly assume the Bernese Alps (Jungfrau/Zermatt area). The peak sits in the Monte Rosa massif on the Italian border.

question: What is the least populous commune in Switzerland, and in which canton is it located?

options.A: Kammersrohr, in the canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden
options.B: Rheinau, in the canton of Zurich
options.C: Rivaz, in the canton of Vaud
options.D: Kammersrohr, in the canton of Solothurn

source_quote: The least populous is Kammersrohr in the canton of Solothurn (32 people)
notes: 32 residents. Counter-intuitive: the least populous commune is in Solothurn, not in an Appenzell or Graubünden mountain canton. Population figures are year-dependent and will drift.

question: Which six cantons are the former half-cantons of Switzerland?

options.A: Obwalden, Nidwalden, Appenzell Ausserrhoden, Appenzell Innerrhoden, Basel Stadt and Geneva
options.B: Schwyz, Uri, Glarus, Zug, Thurgau and Solothurn
options.C: Obwalden, Nidwalden, Appenzell Ausserrhoden, Appenzell Innerrhoden, St. Gallen and Basel Landschaft
options.D: Obwalden, Nidwalden, Appenzell Ausserrhoden, Appenzell Innerrhoden, Basel Stadt and Basel Landschaft

source_quote: The former half-cantons of Obwalden, Nidwalden, Appenzell Ausserrhoden, Appenzell Innerrhoden, Basel Stadt and Basel Landschaft are only entitled to one.
notes: Deliberately tests only the canton-identity half of the S026 fact, framed as the 6/20 structure behind the number 26. The Council of States seat arithmetic (20 cantons with two seats, 46 seats total) is owned by the politics category via S003 and is not asked here. Canton names appear in the German forms printed on the source page.

question: In Switzerland, what is the minimum daily rest period an employer must grant to an employee aged 20 or over between two working days?

options.A: 8 hours
options.B: 11 consecutive hours
options.C: 12 hours
options.D: 10 hours

source_quote: it must last at least 11 consecutive hours
notes: Distractor C is the rule for employees under 18 ('the daily rest period must always be at least 12 hours'); distractor A is the once-a-week reduction the employer may grant if the two-week average is 11 hours.

question: An employee works between 11pm and 6am on fewer than 25 nights per calendar year. What must the employer pay for those nights?

options.A: Time off equal to 10% of the night hours worked
options.B: A wage supplement of at least 10%
options.C: A wage supplement of at least 50%
options.D: A wage supplement of at least 25%

source_quote: A supplement of at least 25% must be paid for work between 11pm and 6am carried out for less than 25 nights per calendar year.
notes: Distractor A is the regime for regular night work (25 or more nights per calendar year), where the compensation is time off equal to 10% of night hours; distractor C is the 50% supplement for occasional Sunday work. Cash payment in lieu of compensatory time off is prohibited.

question: In Switzerland, which level of government is responsible for compulsory education?

options.A: The Confederation, acting through a federal education ministry
options.B: The communes, which set the school system and appoint the teachers
options.C: The cantons
options.D: The cantons jointly with the Confederation, under federal supervision

source_quote: Compulsory education is the responsibility of the cantons. This is why it is important to check the information on your canton's website.
notes: Switzerland has no federal school system — the structural opposite of Germany, Austria and France. Distractor B is scope confusion: communes run individual schools, but the responsibility statement sits with the cantons.

question: Switzerland recycles a high share of its waste, yet materials recovered from waste form only a small share of the country's total material consumption. What are the two figures?

options.A: 70% of total waste volume recycled, but secondary raw materials at 14% of total material consumption
options.B: 70% of total waste volume recycled, and secondary raw materials at 70% of total material consumption
options.C: 14% of total waste volume recycled, and secondary raw materials at 70% of total material consumption
options.D: 53% of municipal solid waste recycled, and secondary raw materials at 14% of total material consumption

source_quote: At present, over two thirds (70%) of Switzerland's total waste volume is recycled. Measured against total material consumption, materials recovered from waste (known as secondary raw materials) make up only a small proportion: 14% in 2019
notes: The 14% figure is from 2019; the 70% recycling rate is 'at present' as published by FOEN. Distractor D uses the municipal-solid-waste rate (53% in 2020), which measures a different quantity. MUNICIPAL-WASTE-VARIABLE: municipal waste figures are administered at commune level.

question: A traveller returning to Switzerland carries goods for personal use with a total value of CHF 400. The tax-free import limit is CHF 150. On what amount is the Swiss import VAT calculated?

options.A: On the excess only — the CHF 250 by which the total value exceeds the CHF 150 limit
options.B: On the whole value — CHF 400
options.C: On the first CHF 150 only
options.D: On nothing, because all the goods are for personal use

source_quote: If the total value exceeds CHF 150, you must pay VAT on the total value of the imported goods. Example: The total value is CHF 400.
notes: Distractor A is the intuitive 'excess only' rule used in many other countries. The verified Swiss tax-free limit is CHF 150 per person per day.

question: What are the Swiss standard VAT rate and the reduced rate that applies to goods such as foodstuffs, books, magazines and medicines?

options.A: 6.7% standard, 2.1% reduced
options.B: 8.1% standard, 3.8% reduced
options.C: 10.0% standard, 2.6% reduced
options.D: 8.1% standard, 2.6% reduced

source_quote: VAT is 8.1%. A reduced rate of 2.6% applies for certain goods (e.g. foodstuffs, including non-alcoholic beverages, books, magazines and medicines).
notes: Distractor A is the pre-2001 Swiss rate pair. Figures as published by the Federal Office for Customs and Border Security at access date 2026-10-12.

question: When the Helvetian Republic was proclaimed in 1798 under French occupation, which institution — described as a predecessor of today's Swiss Federal Archives — was established at the same time?

options.A: the Central Archives
options.B: the Swiss National Library
options.C: the Federal Mint
options.D: the Federal Chancellery

source_quote: The Central Archives, a predecessor of the current Swiss Federal Archives, were also established during this time.
notes: Distractors are all real Swiss federal institutions that simply do not date from 1798.

question: Why was the seat of the Swiss Federal Supreme Court assigned to Lausanne rather than to Zurich, Bern or Lucerne?

options.A: Because Lausanne was the largest city in French-speaking Switzerland.
options.B: As a concession to the French-speaking liberals.
options.C: Because the cantonal government of Vaud paid for the building.
options.D: Because the first president of the court came from Lausanne.

source_quote: As a concession to the French-speaking liberals, the seat of the Swiss Federal Supreme Court was assigned to Lausanne.
notes: A strong trap: the court does have a second site in Lucerne, but Lucerne was never the seat, and neither was Zurich or the federal city Bern.

question: In which year did the Federal Supreme Court move into the Neoclassical building in the Mon-Repos park that still houses it today?
source_quote: Due to the outbreak of the First World War, the new courthouse could not be built until 1922. The striking Neoclassical building in the Mon-Repos park still shapes our image of the Swiss Federal Supreme Court today.
notes: 1887 is the year the court moved into the purpose-built structure on the Esplanade de Montbenon — a deliberate near-miss distractor.

question: On what date did Switzerland's all-male electorate grant the vote to the nation's female citizens?

options.A: 7 February 1971
options.B: 1 February 1959
options.C: 14 June 1971
options.D: 28 April 1991

source_quote: On 7 February 1971, Switzerland's all-male electorate granted the vote to the nation's female citizens.
notes: 1 February 1959 is the first (rejected) federal suffrage vote and 28 April 1991 the Appenzell Innerrhoden cantonal election — both genuine dates used as distractors.

question: The first Geneva Convention, adopted in August 1864, introduced a unified emblem for military medical services. What did that emblem look like?

options.A: a white cross on a red background
options.B: a red cross on a white background
options.C: a red crescent on a white background
options.D: a red cross on a black background

source_quote: And in August 1864 it persuaded governments to adopt the first Geneva Convention. This treaty obliged armies to care for wounded soldiers, whatever side they were on, and introduced a unified emblem for the medical services: a red cross on a white background.
notes: Distractor A is the actual Swiss flag; the emblem is its colour inverse. The source states only the colours, not the inversion — the inverse relationship must be inferred. The red crescent is the real alternative emblem used by the Red Crescent societies.

question: In which years was the International Committee of the Red Cross awarded the Nobel Peace Prize?

options.D: 1917, 1944 and again in 1963, the last together with the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies

source_quote: The ICRC was then awarded the Nobel Prize in 1917 and 1944, as a tribute to its humanitarian activities during the two World Wars, and again in 1963, together with the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies.
notes: The Nobel quote comes from the second ICRC page recorded in the same raw_pages file. Distractor A mixes in Henry Dunant's 1901 prize, which went to him personally, not to the ICRC.

question: On what date did the people and the cantons approve the 1999 total revision of the Federal Constitution?

options.A: 18 April 1999
options.B: 12 September 1848
options.D: 1 January 2000

source_quote: This total revision was approved by the People and the cantons on 18 April 1999 by majorities of 59.2% and 14 out of 26 cantons respectively.
notes: It came into force on 1 January 2000 (distractor D). The quote is from the parlament.ch Federal Constitution page recorded verbatim inside the S048 raw_pages file; ch-info.swiss is the header URL of that file. 14 of 26 cantons is a majority but not an overwhelming one.

question: On what date did Swiss voters approve joining the United Nations?

options.A: 10 March 2002
options.B: 10 September 2002
options.C: 3 March 2002
options.D: 16 March 1986

source_quote: When, on March 3, 2002, the Swiss were again called upon to vote on joining the world body, the decision turned out to be quite close.
notes: Verified: referendum 3 March 2002; the UN General Assembly accepted Switzerland as the 190th member state on 10 September 2002 (distractor B). Distractor A, 10 March 2002, is the disproved date recorded in the verification log. 16 March 1986 was an earlier rejected initiative. swissinfo.ch is the Swiss Broadcasting Corporation, not a federal page.

question: A restaurant guest asks whether they must leave a tip in Switzerland. What is the correct position according to the national tourism organisation's own statement of local custom?

options.A: The guest is not obliged to tip, although paying a tip is customary in many restaurants.
options.B: Tipping is compulsory in restaurants, and the amount is fixed at ten percent of the bill by federal regulation.
options.C: Tipping is compulsory only in Zurich and Geneva, and optional everywhere else in the country.
options.D: The guest is obliged to tip whenever the restaurant has more than five employees.

source_quote: In Switzerland, the guest is not obliged to tip. In many restaurants, however, it is customary to pay a tip.
notes: Swiss-specific: customary but not a legal obligation. Distractors invent a federal fixed rate and cantonal differences that do not exist.

question: The hospitality trade association states that tips are not wages. How should that statement be weighted when answering a question about Swiss law?

options.A: It is settled Swiss law, because the trade association is the sector's competent authority.
options.B: It is settled Swiss law, because it is written into the hospitality sector's collective agreement.
options.C: It carries no weight at all, because a trade association has no standing to interpret employment law.
options.D: It is the association's own position and is contested by labour-law academics, so it cannot be presented as settled law.

source_quote: Grundsätzlich sind Trinkgelder kein Lohn und auch kein Bestandteil davon. Das Gastgewerbe verfügt über einen guten Landes-Gesamtarbeitsvertrag.
notes: A source-criticism item: the answer is about evidential weight. B is the trap - the collective agreement exists but does not settle the point.

question: A Swiss resident buys goods abroad purely for resale in a Swiss shop and brings them back. How are those goods treated at import?

options.A: They are covered by the CHF 150 tax-free limit in the same way as any other purchase made abroad
options.B: They are covered by the tax-free limit as long as their total value stays below CHF 150
options.C: They are subject to VAT
options.D: They are subject to VAT only if their total value exceeds CHF 150

source_quote: Goods that are not intended for your personal use or as gifts are subject to VAT.
notes: The allowance tests purpose first and value second; commercial goods fall outside it at any value. Distractor D is the common confusion of treating value as the only test.

question: A traveller returns with goods that stay below the CHF 150 VAT tax-free limit but exceed the duty-free allowances for alcohol. What is still payable?

options.A: Customs duties
options.B: VAT at the standard rate of 8.1%
options.C: Customs duties and VAT at the reduced rate of 2.6%
options.D: Nothing further, because the CHF 150 limit covers all import charges

source_quote: In addition to VAT, you must pay customs duties if the goods you are carrying exceed the duty-free allowances for alcohol, tobacco products and certain foodstuffs.
notes: The CHF 150 figure is the VAT tax-free limit; the separate duty-free allowances belong to customs duties. Distractor C mixes the two regimes and adds a rate that does not apply to alcohol.

question: A traveller receives a gift abroad and declares it to Swiss customs. On what basis is the import VAT assessed for such a gift?

options.A: On any receipt the giver can produce, or else on a self-declared value
options.B: Its market value
options.C: On the nominal value printed on the gift packaging, where one exists
options.D: On the recipient's own estimate of what the gift is worth to them personally

source_quote: Otherwise, the market value is taxed, e.g. in the case of gifts. The market value refers to the sum a third party would have had to pay to buy the item.
notes: Purchases are taxed on the invoice, receipt or purchase contract; where there is none - gifts in particular - the market value applies, i.e. what a third party would have paid. Traps are the self-declared value and the recipient's sentimental valuation.

question: Roughly how much waste does Switzerland generate in a year, according to the Federal Office for the Environment?

options.A: About 8 to 9 million tonnes
options.B: About 30 million tonnes
options.C: About 80 to 90 million tonnes
options.D: About 300 million tonnes

source_quote: Overall, Switzerland generates about 80 to 90 million tonnes of waste annually, and it is fair to assume that the total quantity will continue to rise in the future.
notes: Order-of-magnitude anchor for the whole waste topic: the headline recycling rate makes Swiss volumes sound modest, but construction and demolition account for the great majority. Distractors straddle the correct figure by roughly a decade each.

question: On which principle is the financing of waste disposal in Switzerland based?

options.A: Waste disposal is financed from general federal tax revenue collected centrally
options.B: The 'polluter pays' principle
options.C: The cantons and communes must cover the full cost of disposal from their own budgets
options.D: Producers of packaged goods finance disposal through a federal levy on packaging

source_quote: The disposal of all waste costs Switzerland a good CHF 3 billion a year. The 'polluter pays' principle is widely applied in Switzerland, i.e. whoever creates the waste must also pay for its disposal.
notes: The named principle matters more than the CHF 3 billion figure: whoever creates the waste pays for its disposal. Traps are the centrally funded reading and the producer-llevy model, neither of which is the stated basis.

question: In Switzerland, admission to a baccalaureate school depends on which factor?

options.A: The Confederation alone, under a uniform federal admission rule
options.B: The commune alone, through a single entrance test for all cantons
options.C: The canton and the type of baccalaureate
options.D: The federal institute of technology the pupil intends to attend afterwards

source_quote: If you want to study for a baccalaureate, you need to meet different requirements depending on the canton and the type of baccalaureate you wish to obtain, including good grades, a recommendation from your class teacher or a successful entrance examination.
notes: Entry is cantonal and type-dependent: good grades, a class teacher's recommendation or an entrance examination. Traps are the assumption of a single federal rule and the assumption that grades alone decide.

question: Under Swiss rules, who is responsible for getting a child to school, and when may a commune step in?

options.A: The parents, with commune support only where the route is very long or too dangerous
options.B: The commune, which must provide transport for any child living more than two kilometres from school
options.C: The canton, which arranges school transport for every child in its territory
options.D: The parents, with commune transport guaranteed for any child of compulsory-school age

source_quote: Getting a child to school is the responsibility of the parents. The communes only provide support if the route to school is very long or too dangerous.
notes: Communes step in only for a very long or dangerous route, which is what Pedibus-style schemes address. The over-general distractor D sounds like a parental duty with municipal backing and is the trap for those who half-remember the rule.

question: Alongside organising federal elections and popular votes, which parties submit the signatures they have collected to the Federal Chancellery?

options.A: The Federal Supreme Court
options.B: Members of the Federal Assembly acting in united chambers
options.C: Referendum and initiative committees
options.D: The cantonal governments

source_quote: Along with the cantons, the Federal Chancellery organises federal elections and popular votes. Referendum and initiative committees submit the signatures they collect to the Federal Chancellery.
notes: Separates the Chancellery's organising role from its intake role, and separates both from the cantons' own task of organising the vote.

question: A case concerns money laundering and organised crime with an international dimension. Which federal body hears such cases?

options.A: The Federal Supreme Court sitting as a criminal first-instance court
options.B: The Federal Criminal Court
options.C: The Federal Administrative Court
options.D: The Federal Patent Court

source_quote: The Federal Criminal Court hears criminal cases involving offences against federal interests, explosives offences, international cases of white-collar crime, cases relating to organised crime, corruption and money laundering, and offences related to civil aviation or war material.
notes: Distinguishes the four federal courts by subject matter. D invents a criminal first-instance division of the Supreme Court, a structure familiar from other countries.

question: A member of a cantonal government privately disagrees with a decision the government has taken. What is that member required to do?

options.A: Ask the cantonal parliament to reverse the decision
options.B: Abstain in public and distance themselves from the decision
options.C: Defend the government's position publicly, whatever their own opinion
options.D: Resign from the cantonal government immediately

source_quote: All members of the cantonal government must defend the position of the collegial body, regardless of their personal opinion.
notes: Collegiality binds the cantonal government exactly as it binds the Federal Council; B, C and D are all plausible reactions from a cabinet-style mental model.

question: In which cantons do foreign nationals have the right to vote at cantonal level, though not to stand for election?

options.A: Jura and Geneva
options.B: Neuchâtel and Basel-Stadt
options.C: Geneva and Vaud
options.D: Jura and Neuchâtel

source_quote: At the cantonal level, Jura and Neuchâtel grant the right to vote (but not to stand for election) to foreign nationals.
notes: High search cost and tests real cantonal variation; Geneva and Vaud are the intuitive French-speaking guesses and are not the cited pair.

question: Does a Swiss citizen living in Switzerland have to register in order to be entered on the electoral roll of their commune?

options.A: Yes, but only people holding a single nationality
options.B: No, the commune adds them automatically
options.C: Yes, at the commune's population office each year
options.D: Yes, with the cantonal government before the vote

source_quote: If you live in Switzerland, you do not need to register to vote: you will be added to the electoral register of your commune of residence as a matter of course as soon as you fulfil the conditions for being eligible to vote.
notes: Contrast with the explicit registration required of Swiss citizens abroad; an automatic-register premise is unusual compared with most EU systems.

question: Can a federal popular initiative be used at federal level to demand a change to an existing federal law rather than to the Constitution?

options.A: Yes, but only for laws adopted before the entry into force of the 1999 Constitution
options.B: Yes, provided the Federal Assembly agrees to treat the proposal as constitutional
options.C: No, a federal popular initiative can concern only the Constitution
options.D: Yes, if the initiative is supported by a majority of the cantons

source_quote: A federal popular initiative concerns only the Constitution. In contrast to the position in some cantons, there is no procedure at federal level for amending existing laws or introducing new laws through an initiative.
notes: The sharpest federalism point in the corpus: some cantons have legislative initiatives, federal level does not. C and D invent conditional routes.

question: How far in advance of the vote on a federal popular initiative must the date be announced, and by whom?

options.A: The cantonal governments must announce it at least one year ahead
options.B: The Federal Council must announce it at least four months ahead
options.C: The Federal Assembly must announce it at least six months ahead
options.D: The Federal Chancellery must announce it at least three months ahead

source_quote: The Federal Council must announce the date of the vote at least four months in advance.
notes: The executive, not the Chancellery or Parliament, fixes the ballot date; C is the natural confusion with the Chancellery's vote-organising role.

question: Parliament decides not only on laws but also on enactments that are not laws, such as decisions on international treaties. Can an optional referendum be launched against such a decision?

options.A: Yes, an optional referendum is possible
options.B: No, only amendments to the Constitution are put to a vote
options.C: No, because treaties are approved by the Federal Council alone
options.D: Yes, but only after a majority of the cantons has approved the treaty

source_quote: Parliament also decides on enactments that are not laws, for example decisions on international treaties between Switzerland and other countries. It is also possible to launch an optional referendum against these.
notes: The referendum right reaches further than formally legislated acts; B and C are the usual assumptions about treaty approval in a parliamentary system.

question: Two groups from different political camps both want to challenge the same federal law. How is that handled?

options.A: Both may initiate a referendum, but their signatures are counted separately
options.B: Only one group may challenge the law if the camps disagree
options.C: Both may initiate a referendum, and their signatures are counted
options.D: Only the group that registered first may challenge the law

source_quote: What is more, several groups can initiate a referendum against the same new or amended law – even though they might be from different political camps. The signatures collected are counted.
notes: Competing committees do not exclude each other; C is a near-miss that would also work in practice but is not what the page states.

question: Under Swiss data protection law, what is actually protected?

options.A: The data themselves, as an asset of whoever holds them
options.B: The persons about whom data are processed
options.C: The commercial value of the collected information
options.D: Only special categories of personal data, such as health and criminal records

source_quote: Data protection law does not protect data as such, but rather the persons about whom data is processed.
notes: Traps the property-framing imported from data-protection-as-asset models; the FDPIC states the protection attaches to persons, not to the data as a commodity.

question: Under Swiss law, how does the processing of personal data by private entities generally stand?

options.A: It is prohibited unless the data subject has given prior written consent
options.B: It is permitted only where the data have been fully anonymised
options.C: It requires prior authorisation from the FDPIC for each processing purpose
options.D: It is permitted in principle, with the test being whether the invasion of privacy can be justified by consent or by overriding interests

source_quote: The situation is different for the processing of personal data by private entities. In principle, this is permitted in Switzerland.
notes: Distractor A is the GDPR prior-consent default, which does not carry over to Swiss private-sector processing; the source deliberately does not use the words opt-in or opt-out.

question: The duty to inform under Swiss data protection law is not absolute. How are its exceptions treated?

options.A: They are drawn broadly by the FDPIC and may be relied on at the controller's discretion
options.B: They cover, for example, a data subject who already has the information or processing required by law, and they must be narrowly interpreted
options.C: They apply only where a federal authority processes the data
options.D: They apply only to special categories of data such as health data

source_quote: Moreover, the exceptions mentioned in Article 20 FADP limit or remove the duty to provide information, for example if a data subject already has the information (because they previously consented to their data being processed) or if the processing of personal data is required by law. These exceptions must be narrowly interpreted: the data controller should not assume that they will apply.
notes: Names the Article 20 FADP exceptions and the narrow-interpretation rule; distractor A is the opposite of the FDPIC's express warning against assuming they apply.

question: Which residence permit categories are issued as biometric residence permits for foreign nationals in Switzerland?

options.A: Short-term residence permits (L), residence permits (B) and settlement permits (C)
options.B: All residence permits without exception, including the N permit for asylum seekers and the F permit for provisionally admitted foreigners
options.C: Only residence permits (B), because short stays are covered by a passport stamp
options.D: Only settlement permits (C), since biometric data are required for a permanent status

source_quote: Biometric residence permits shall be issued to holders of the following categories of residence permit: - Short-term residence permits (L) - Residence permits (B) - Settlement permits (C)
notes: Exactly the three categories L, B and C; the N and F permits are deliberately not in the biometric programme.

question: Who decides the application procedure for a biometric residence permit in Switzerland, and who captures the biometric data?

options.A: The SEM decides nationally, and the fingerprints are taken at the Swiss embassy
options.B: The municipality of residence decides, and the data are captured by the cantonal police
options.C: The FDPIC decides, and the data are captured by an accredited private provider
options.D: The canton of residence decides, and the biometric data are captured by that canton's authority

source_quote: The application procedure and issuance of a biometric residence permit are decided by the Canton of residence. Biometric data are obtained from the person by the corresponding authority in the Canton of residence.
notes: Cantonal variable: no single national procedure or fee. Distractor A overstates the SEM's role, which is limited to centrally producing the cards.

question: An EU/EFTA national's B residence permit comes up for renewal after more than twelve consecutive months of involuntary unemployment. How may that first renewal be dealt with?

options.A: It may be limited to one year
options.B: It cannot be granted at all, because the holder no longer has gainful employment
options.C: It must be reduced to the three-month minimum used for short-stay permits
options.D: It is automatically replaced by an L permit issued to job seekers

source_quote: First-time renewal of the permit can be limited to one year, however, if the holder has been involuntarily unemployed for more than twelve consecutive months.
notes: A shortening mechanism, not a withdrawal rule. Distractors B and D over-read the unemployment fact into loss of status or an automatic category change.

question: An EU/EFTA national takes up a series of engagements in Switzerland, none lasting longer than three months. How are these handled?

options.A: Each engagement requires its own work permit of up to three months
options.B: A G cross-border commuter permit is required throughout
options.C: A B residence permit valid for twelve months is required
options.D: Contracts of less than three months' duration within a calendar year are not subject to a permit but are regulated via the online notification procedure

source_quote: Employment contracts of less than three months' duration within a calendar year are not subject to a permit but are regulated via the online notification procedure.
notes: The Swiss online notification procedure replaces a permit for short engagements below three months within a calendar year; the boundary is three months, not one year.

question: Beyond Switzerland's single national public holiday, who determines the other public holidays observed in a canton?

options.A: The federal government, which publishes a national list each year
options.B: Each canton, which can have up to eight additional public holidays on its territory
options.C: Each commune alone, with no upper limit and no cantonal role
options.D: The cantons and communes jointly, up to a federal ceiling of eight

source_quote: The cantons can each have up to eight additional public holidays on their territory. Public holidays can thus vary from canton to canton.
notes: Eight is a ceiling on the cantonal additions, not a nationwide total of public holidays; distractor D misreads it as a federal maximum.

question: According to the Canton Bern conciliation authority, when is an ordinary termination of a tenancy possible?

options.A: Only if the notice period and the locally customary termination dates are observed
options.B: On one month's notice, aligned to the end of a calendar month
options.C: Only with the prior consent of the conciliation authority
options.D: Only for a fixed-term contract, never for an open-ended one

source_quote: Die ordentliche Kündigung ist nur unter Einhaltung der Kündigungsfrist und der Kündigungstermine möglich.
notes: Source quote is German. The source states the locally customary termination dates, not a universal end-of-month rule, so distractor B is the widely repeated but unverified one-month claim.

question: Within what period after giving birth is a mother in Switzerland not allowed to return to work?

options.A: The first four weeks after the birth
options.B: The first eight weeks after the birth
options.C: The first twelve weeks after the birth
options.D: The first six weeks after the birth

source_quote: You are not allowed to return to work in the first eight weeks after the birth.
notes: Traps confusion with the 14-week maternity leave itself and with the 16-week dismissal protection; 4/6/12 weeks are the plausible wrong figures.

question: A mother in Switzerland extends her maternity leave by the two weeks available beyond the standard 14-week period. What does she receive for those two additional weeks?

options.A: Maternity allowance at half the usual rate
options.B: The same maternity allowance as for the first 14 weeks
options.C: Maternity allowance at 80% of earnings, capped at CHF 220 per day
options.D: Nothing - no benefits are paid for the two additional weeks

source_quote: You have the right to extend your maternity leave by two weeks beyond the standard 14-week period. However, you will not receive benefits for those two additional weeks.
notes: Traps the 80%/CHF 220 allowance figures lifted from the standard maternity allowance rule; the extension is unpaid.

question: Which group is not subject to the mandatory Swiss LPP/BVG occupational benefits scheme?

options.A: Salaried persons with a job contract of unlimited duration
options.B: The self-employed
options.C: Salaried persons working at least 50 per cent of full time for a company
options.D: Salaried persons on contracts longer than three months

source_quote: Certain groups of people are not subject to the mandatory scheme: the self-employed, salaried persons with a job contract that does not exceed three months, family members of a person operating an agricultural establishment in which they are employed, persons who are disabled to at least 70 % according to the provisions of the AI.
notes: The other three exempt groups (short contracts, agricultural family members, 70 % disabled) are real exemptions, so a distractor naming any of them would also be defensible; instead the distractors name categories that ARE covered, which is what a non-expert would wrongly believe.

question: Under the Swiss LPP/BVG, from what point are additional retirement savings made for an employee?

options.A: From the employee's 17th birthday
options.B: From 1 January after the employee reaches the age of 20
options.C: From 1 January after the employee reaches the age of 24
options.D: From the employee's 18th birthday

source_quote: The obligation to take out insurance sets in with gainful employment, after reaching 17 at the earliest. Until the employee reaches the age of 24, contributions only cover the risks of death and disability. From 1 January after the employee reaches the age of 24, additional savings are made for the retirement pension.
notes: Traps the two other ages on the same passage (17 = entry into the scheme, 18 = entry into savings elsewhere framed), and the off-by-one of 'at 24' vs 'from the 1 January after 24'.

question: How does the Swiss state contribute to the financing of second-pillar pension funds?

options.A: By paying a fixed share of each fund's annual expenditure
options.B: By guaranteeing the conversion factor used when the accumulated capital is turned into a pension
options.C: By paying a direct per-person annual subsidy into the fund of the person's employer
options.D: Only indirectly, by granting tax exemption on the contributions and on second-pillar assets

source_quote: The state contributes only indirectly to the financing of pension funds, by granting tax exemption on the contributions and 2nd pillar assets.
notes: Traps the assumption that the state co-funds the second pillar like it does the first; tax exemption is the only state support the page describes.

question: Under the collective financing principle of the LPP/BVG, what must an employer's contribution be?

options.A: At least equal to the sum of contributions paid by all the employees
options.B: At least half of the sum of contributions paid by all the employees
options.C: Equal to that individual employee's contribution and to no more
options.D: Any amount agreed with the fund, provided it is disclosed in the fund's accounts

source_quote: The LPP/BVG is based on the principle of collective financing: the contribution of the employer must be at least equal to the sum of contributions paid by all the employees.
notes: Traps the common belief that the employer pays exactly the employee's own share, and the 50/50-style split that belongs to OASI.

question: Under the OASI, from when must a person resident in Switzerland pay contributions, and how does that differ for someone already in paid work?

options.A: From 1 January after turning 18 in all cases; for those already working, from 1 January of the year in which they turn 16
options.B: From 1 January after turning 25 in all cases; for those already working, from 1 January of the year in which they turn 20
options.C: From the age of 20, but only for those in paid employment; non-employed persons begin at 25
options.D: From 1 January after turning 20; for those already working, from 1 January of the year in which they turn 18

source_quote: If you live or work in Switzerland, you must pay OASI contributions from 1 January after you turn 20 until you reach the reference (retirement) age. If you are already working, this obligation begins on 1 January of the year in which you turn 18.
notes: Two-age item with an inverted rule: the working person starts EARLIER (18) than the general rule (20). Distractors transplant 16/20/25 and impose a paid-employment condition the page rejects.

question: Once the annual deductible has been used up in Swiss compulsory health insurance, what share of healthcare costs does the insured person still pay?

options.A: Twenty per cent, capped at CHF 1,400 per year
options.B: Ten per cent, capped at CHF 700 per year
options.C: Ten per cent, with no annual cap
options.D: Five per cent, capped at CHF 350 per year

source_quote: When the deductible has been used up you will still pay ten percent of your healthcare costs. However, this retention fee is limited to CHF 700 per year (CHF 350 for children).
notes: Two-figure item (coinsurance rate + annual cap). CHF 350 is the child cap, a confident wrong pick for an adult; 'no cap' is the other common misconception.

question: Premiums for compulsory basic health insurance in Switzerland are lower for which group?

options.A: People over the age of 65
options.B: Employees who work at least eight hours per week
options.C: Insured persons who choose the CHF 2,500 deductible
options.D: Children and young adults under the age of 25

source_quote: Premiums are lower for children and young adults under the age of 25.
notes: Traps the pensionable-age intuition that premiums fall after 65, which is where most countries' premium relief goes.

question: In the Council of States, how many cantons are entitled to two seats?

options.A: 6 cantons
options.B: 26 cantons
options.C: 20 cantons
options.D: 13 cantons

source_quote: In the Council of States, 20 cantons are entitled to two seats.
notes: Half-canton trap: models frequently answer 26 (one seat per canton is not the rule) or 6 (counting only the former half-cantons). 20 two-seat cantons plus 6 one-seat cantons is the structure behind the chamber's 46 seats.

question: Which of the following cantons is entitled to two seats in the Council of States?

options.A: Appenzell Innerrhoden
options.B: Glarus
options.C: Nidwalden
options.D: Basel-Stadt

source_quote: Two seats: Aargau, Bern, Freiburg, Geneva, Glarus, Graubünden, Jura, Luzern, Neuchâtel, Schaffhausen, Schwyz, Solothurn, St. Gallen, Thurgau, Ticino, Uri, Vaud, Valais, Zug, Zurich.
notes: All three distractors appear on the same page under 'One seat', so the item tests membership of the 20-canton list rather than the six half-cantons already asked at K080/K006. Glarus is one of the smallest cantons by population yet still holds two upper-chamber seats, which is the counter-intuitive point.

question: With which of Switzerland's other national languages does Romansh share a Latin origin?

options.A: Italian and French
options.B: German and Italian
options.C: German and French
options.D: None — Romansh is Germanic in origin

source_quote: Rumantsch, like Italian and French, is a language with Latin roots.
notes: The strongest misconception trap in the language set: because Switzerland is majority-German-speaking, models place Romansh in the Germanic family. It groups with the Romance languages, not with German.

question: In the Swiss hierarchy of norms, what does the Federal Constitution take precedence over?

options.A: Cantonal constitutions only
options.B: Federal laws adopted before the 1999 total revision
options.C: Cantonal laws, but not communal ordinances
options.D: All laws and ordinances of the Confederation, the cantons and the communes

source_quote: The Federal Constitution is the highest law of Switzerland. It takes precedence over all laws and ordinances of the Confederation, cantons and communes.
notes: The three-level bite is what makes this hard: a federal constitution outranking not only federal statutes but cantonal and communal law too. Option A confuses constitutional rank with cantonal constitutional autonomy (tested at K255).

question: Since when has Romansh been recognised in the Swiss Constitution as a national language?
source_quote: Since 1938 Romansh has been recognised in the Swiss Constitution as a national language along with German, French and Italian.
notes: 1848 is the federal-state date and 1979 the admission of Jura; both are confident wrong picks. The four-national-language set itself is asked at K061.

question: Switzerland's commune count is falling through mergers, so published figures differ by publication date. In the undated CH Info brochure cited by the source file, into how many communes are the 26 cantons divided?

options.A: 26 communes
options.B: 2,110 communes
options.C: 2,121 communes
options.D: About 2,000 communes

source_quote: The 26 cantons are divided into 2110 communes.
notes: Tests whether the model attributes a commune count to its publication rather than treating it as a fixed fact. The corpus deliberately carries several snapshots: 2,110 here (undated CH Info), and 2,121 as of 1 January 2025 in K070 (SWI swissinfo.ch). Both are correct for their own publication; neither is the answer without the attribution. If a future revision of this corpus drops one of the two, drop the other too - two bare commune counts in one benchmark read as an internal contradiction.

question: Which of Switzerland's five neighbours shares the shortest stretch of border with it?

options.A: Austria
options.B: Germany
options.C: Liechtenstein
options.D: France

source_quote: Borders: altogether: 1852 km/Austria 164 km/France 573 km/Germany 334 km/Italy 740 km/Liechtenstein 41 km
notes: Mirror image of K066, which asks for the longest border (Italy). Austria at 164 km is the confident wrong pick because it is the smallest of the 'big four'. Per-country border lengths vary with the measurement or border-survey basis, per the registry note.

question: Following the defeat of Napoleon, what did the great European powers do to Switzerland's borders in 1815?

options.A: They extended them southward to include the whole of the canton of Ticino.
options.B: They fixed them at the Rhine and the Alps, and added the principality of Vaduz.
options.C: They granted Switzerland a permanent corridor to the Adriatic through the Gotthard.
options.D: They set Switzerland's borders as they are today.

source_quote: With the defeat of Napoleon, the great European powers recognised Swiss neutrality and set Switzerland's borders as they are today.
notes: B is the Liechtenstein trap and conflates the 1815 settlement with Liechtenstein's 1806 entry into the French sphere; A and C are the 'Alpine fortress with an outlet' fantasy that models reach for. Borders AND neutrality were settled together in 1815, which is the point of the item.

question: Under the 1907 Hague Conventions, what did neutral states owe in exchange for the inviolability of their territory?

options.A: The right to supply arms and troops to whichever belligerent paid for them.
options.B: An obligation to grant belligerents the use of their airspace and ports.
options.C: A duty to stay out of wars, to treat all belligerents equally, and not to supply them with arms or troops.
options.D: A duty to enforce the peace settlement on both sides of the conflict.

source_quote: In exchange for the inviolability of their territory, such countries were, among other things, bound to stay out of wars, to treat all belligerents equally and not to supply them with arms or troops.
notes: A and B treat neutrality as commerce and access, which is exactly the misunderstanding: neutrality is a reciprocity, not a trade. K120 asks which treaty first codified these rights; this item asks what the bargain was, so the two do not overlap. Quote comes from the swissinfo.ch page recorded in the S050 file.

question: Which body did the Red Cross national societies found in 1919 as the future coordinating and support body of the Movement?

options.A: the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
options.B: the League of Nations' humanitarian commission
options.C: the League of Red Cross Societies
options.D: the International Committee of the Red Cross

source_quote: In 1919, they founded the League of Red Cross Societies, intended as the future coordinating and support body for the Movement.
notes: The International Federation also dates from 1919, so A matches on the year and is the strongest trap in this item; the ICRC (D) appears in the same page and never founded it. This is the most confused corner of the Movement's institutional history and is a Swiss-specific fact rather than a European generality.

question: How many agreements made up the first series of Swiss bilateral agreements with the EU, approved by voters in 2000?
source_quote: The first series of bilateral agreements was accepted by 67% of Swiss voters in 2000. The 7 agreements mainly cover economic matters.
notes: 9 is the count for the second series of 2005, which contains Schengen-Dublin - the two series are routinely swapped, and K113 already used the second series. Switzerland's EU relations run on over 100 bilateral agreements, which invites a larger number than either series.

question: In the sequence of Swiss constitutional development described by the Federal Chancellery, what stage came immediately before the federal state?

options.A: the Helvetian Republic
options.B: a permanent Federal Diet representing 22 cantons
options.C: a confederation of states
options.D: an Austrian crown land under Habsburg administration

source_quote: Switzerland developed over the centuries from a collection of different alliances to a confederation of states and finally to the federal state we know today.
notes: The three-stage sequence alliances then confederation of states then federal state is the point; A is the real 1798 interlude but not the immediate predecessor in this chain, and C and D are generic European-state inventions with no Swiss referent.

question: Why did the surrounding German-speaking regions come to refer to all Swiss confederates by the name of a single canton?

options.A: Because Schwyz was the largest of the three founding cantons.
options.B: Because Uri was the seat of the Federal Diet and issued the earliest federal charters.
options.C: Because the Schwyzers were famous for their role in the Waldstätte Alliance and for their mercenary troops.
options.D: Because Unterwalden supplied the largest contingent to the Swiss armies serving abroad.

source_quote: The Schwyzer, or Switzers, soon became well known far and wide thanks to the significant role they played in the Waldstätte Alliance and the importance of their troops as mercenaries. As a result, the surrounding German-speaking regions started to refer to all confederates as “Schwyzer”.
notes: A is the natural-sounding wrong answer: Schwyz is the canton named, but the source credits role and mercenaries, not size, and the etymology runs from “Schwyzer” to “Schweizer”. C and D attach the distinction to the other two founding cantons. K101 already used the 1291 alliance from this page, so this is a different fact from the same source.

question: Swiss mercenary service was outlawed in connection with which event?

options.A: the Congress of Vienna of 1815
options.B: the proclamation of the Helvetian Republic in 1798
options.C: the founding of the Federal State
options.D: the adoption of the first Geneva Convention in 1864

source_quote: The mercenaries had their heyday between the 15th and 18th century before being outlawed with the founding of the Federal State.
notes: A and B are the two big Swiss constitutional turning points and both are wrong here; D is a Swiss-adjacent date that appears on a different page entirely. The same sentence dates the heyday to the 15th to 18th century, so the two halves of the fact travel together.
